question: What does the treatment do for people right at the cutoff?

okeeffe2025.cite: O’Keeffe & Petersen (2025). Regression discontinuity designs in epidemiology: a practical guide. Clinical Epidemiology 17: 845–862.
okeeffe2025.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC12581866) on 20 Nov 2026; the web text has no page numbers, so places are given as its section headings; in-text reference numbers are left out. The card's own reference (Thistlethwaite & Campbell 1960) is not open access and was not read

steps.title: Find the rule
steps.text: Look for a treatment given by a rule on a continuous score, such as statins from a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10%.

quotes.text: This variable is then compared to a pre-defined, external, threshold that is used to determine treatment

steps.title: Check the jump
steps.text: The chance of being treated must jump at the cutoff: from 0 to 1 if the rule is always followed (sharp), by less if not (fuzzy).

quotes.text: This is known as a “sharp RDD” – where the threshold is a strict separator for the “treated” (above threshold) and “untreated” (below threshold) groups.
If we do not see a discontinuity at the threshold, we cannot apply the RDD design.

steps.title: No sorting
steps.text: People must not be able to nudge their score across the line. A pile-up of scores just on one side is a warning.

quotes.text: We also assume that an individual cannot manipulate their own assignment variable in an effort to place them above (or below) the threshold and then receive (or not receive) the treatment/intervention.

steps.title: Look near the line
steps.text: Just either side of the cutoff, people are nearly the same; only the rule separates them. Check that their other characteristics balance.

quotes.text: This assumption implies that we consider the threshold to be a quasi-randomising device and that groups either side of the threshold can viewed as similar to randomised groups in a two-group individually randomised RCT.

steps.title: Fit each side
steps.text: Fit the outcome against the score separately below and above the cutoff, within a window around it.

quotes.text: The continuity-based method for RDD uses flexible models for the relationship between the assignment variable and outcome, separately on each side of the threshold.

steps.title: Read the jump
steps.text: The gap between the two fits at the cutoff is the effect. It holds for people near the cutoff, not for everyone.

quotes.text: an effect estimate at the threshold that will be formed using data from individuals with assignment variable values within a small window around the threshold.

external-validity.text: It is important to remember that the treatment/intervention effect estimate is valid only in a region around the threshold: the RDD does not estimate a global treatment/intervention effect.

exercise.title: How wide a window?
exercise.intro: Each dot is a patient with a 10-year risk score from 0 to 20%; statins are given from 10%, and they lower the outcome. Compare everyone treated with everyone untreated, then fit a line each side near the cutoff and change the window.
exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise with a fixed seed (a sharp rule: everyone at or above 10% is treated); the true effect is built in, so you can check each estimate against it.

limits: The card's defining paper (Thistlethwaite & Campbell 1960) and its example (Angrist & Lavy 1999, Maimonides' rule) were not read for this page.
The exercise uses a sharp rule and plain straight lines; O’Keeffe & Petersen (2025) also cover fuzzy designs, data-driven bandwidths and local randomisation, which it does not show.
